name: Glycopyrronium tosylate (Qbrexza)

lead: Qbrexza is a once-daily prescription cloth that cuts heavy underarm sweating, so users keep clothes free of sweat marks and feel more at ease in social settings.

It blocks the muscarinic receptors that signal sweat glands to produce sweat, with limited absorption into the bloodstream. The FDA approved it in June 2018 for ages 9 and up, and Japan approved it in 2022. Two randomised 4-week phase 3 trials, ATMOS-1 and ATMOS-2, found it reduced sweating more than vehicle, and a 44-week open-label study followed.

paras: It is wiped across clean, dry underarms once a day. People typically notice drier underarms within the first weeks of use.
Dry mouth and local skin reactions are described, and case reports describe pupil dilation from transfer to the eye. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Qbrexza is a once-daily underarm wipe that cuts heavy underarm sweating, so users keep clothes free of sweat marks and feel more at ease in social settings. It blocks the signal to the sweat glands. It is FDA-approved for axillary hyperhidrosis and supported by phase 3 trials.

lead: Glycopyrronium tosylate is a topical anticholinergic applied as a once-daily cloth to the underarms for primary axillary hyperhidrosis. Sold in the US as Qbrexza (2.4 percent cloth), it was approved by the FDA in June 2018 for people aged 9 and older and in Japan in January 2022 [1][2].

Its approval rests on two replicate phase 3 trials, ATMOS-1 and ATMOS-2, which compared 3.75 percent glycopyrronium tosylate with vehicle for 4 weeks and found it reduced sweating severity and production versus vehicle [3][4]. A 44-week open-label extension and pediatric analyses followed [5][6].

paras: It blocks muscarinic receptors on eccrine sweat glands. A pharmacokinetic study reported limited systemic exposure with topical use [7].

Reviews describe anticholinergic effects such as dry mouth and local skin reactions [8]. A multicenter case series characterised pharmacologic mydriasis (pupil dilation) after the drug reached the eyes from the cloths [9].

ATMOS-1 and ATMOS-2 were randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled 4-week phase 3 trials [3]. Patient-reported outcomes from the trials were published separately [4]. A 44-week open-label extension assessed longer-term safety [5], post hoc analyses covered pediatric patients [6], and a Japanese randomised study has been reported [10]. Registered trials have also explored palmar hyperhidrosis [11].
